σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd³), τ = 16T/(πd³), σ<sub>a</sub> = 4P/(πd²)
T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) (maximum shear stress theory); τ = 16T<sub>e</sub>/(πd³)
M<sub>e</sub> = ½[M + √(M² + T²)] (maximum normal stress theory); σ = 32M<sub>e</sub>/(πd³)
use K<sub>b</sub> M and K<sub>t</sub> T; τ<sub>allow</sub> = smaller of 0.30S<sub>yt</sub> and 0.18S<sub>ut</sub>, × 0.75 with a keyway
d³ becomes d<sub>o</sub>³(1 − k⁴), k = d<sub>i</sub>/d<sub>o</sub>

N<sub>c</sub> = (60/2π)√(g/δ) rpm, δ in m
1/N<sub>c</sub>² = 1/N<sub>1</sub>² + 1/N<sub>2</sub>² + … + 1/N<sub>s</sub>² (slightly low)
ω<sub>n</sub> = √(g ΣW y/ΣW y²) (slightly high)
F = 2T/d; τ = F/(wl); σ<sub>c</sub> = F/((h/2)l)
T = p n h l R<sub>m</sub>, h = (D − d)/2, R<sub>m</sub> = (D + d)/4
F = 2T/(nD<sub>1</sub>); τ = F/(πd<sub>b</sub>²/4); σ<sub>c</sub> = F/(d<sub>b</sub> t)
T = μWn(r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2; p<sub>max</sub> = W/(2πr<sub>i</sub>(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>))
T = (2/3)μWn(r<sub>o</sub>³ − r<sub>i</sub>³)/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)
T = μNr; E = Tω<sub>rel</sub> t (mean slip speed if it falls to zero)
t, B = 4t, H = 5t; A = 11t², k<sub>xx</sub>² = 3.17t²
P<sub>cr</sub> = σ<sub>c</sub> A/(1 + a(L/k)²), a = 1/7500 for steel
F<sub>p</sub> = d l p<sub>b</sub>; crankpin and piston pin

takeaways: A shaft is sized at the section with the largest bending moment and torque, from the equivalent torque (ductile steel) or the equivalent bending moment, whichever gives the larger diameter.
The ASME code multiplies M and T by shock factors and limits τ to the smaller of 0.30S<sub>yt</sub> and 0.18S<sub>ut</sub>, cut by a quarter for a keyway.
An axial load changes σ<sub>x</sub>, so the maximum shear stress must be found from σ<sub>b</sub> + σ<sub>a</sub> on the side where they add, not from T<sub>e</sub>.
Long or fast shafts are often decided by twist, deflection or critical speed, not stress; run at least 20 to 25 % away from N<sub>c</sub>.
A key is checked in shear on w × l and in crushing on (h/2) × l; for a rectangular key crushing usually needs the longer length.
A flange coupling is checked link by link: shaft, key, hub, flange and bolts. A bushed pin must also pass a bending check.
Clutch torque is μWn times a friction radius; uniform wear gives the lower, design value.
A connecting rod is a column: Rankine’s formula about the xx axis with a factor of safety of 5 to 6 sets its I-section, and bearing pressure sets its ends.
A crankshaft is checked at top dead centre (bending) and at maximum torque (bending plus torsion); the crankpin must pass both bearing and bending checks.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask long questions as full design calculations: a shaft by the ASME code with a rigidity or critical-speed check, a key, a protected flange or bushed-pin coupling, and, in the engine-components part of the course, a connecting rod and a centre crankshaft. Write the formula, substitute with units, round up to a standard size and close with a check.

bank.q: Derive the equivalent torque and the equivalent bending moment for a solid shaft under a bending moment M and a torque T, name the failure theory behind each, and find the diameter for M = 500 N·m and T = 400 N·m with τ<sub>allow</sub> = 40 MPa and σ<sub>allow</sub> = 80 MPa.
outline: Maximum shear stress theory gives T<sub>e</sub>
Maximum normal stress theory gives M<sub>e</sub>
answer: Data and aim: a solid shaft of diameter d carries a bending moment M and a torque T at the same section. We want a single equivalent load for each failure theory, then the diameter for M = 500 N·m, T = 400 N·m, τ<sub>allow</sub> = 40 MPa and σ<sub>allow</sub> = 80 MPa.

At the outer surface the bending stress along the axis is σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd³) (from σ = M/Z with Z = πd³/32) and the torsional shear stress is τ = 16T/(πd³) (from τ = T/Z<sub>p</sub> with Z<sub>p</sub> = πd³/16). The radial stress is zero, so the element is in plane stress with σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> = 0 and τ<sub>xy</sub> = τ.

answer.text: Maximum shear stress theory (Guest), for ductile material: substitute σ<sub>b</sub> and τ in τ<sub>max</sub>.
answer.pre:
τ<sub>max</sub> = √((16M/πd³)² + (16T/πd³)²) = (16/πd³)√(M² + T²)
so T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²) and τ<sub>allow</sub> = 16T<sub>e</sub>/(πd³)

answer: T<sub>e</sub> is the torque that, acting alone, would cause the same maximum shear stress as M and T together.

answer.text: Maximum normal stress theory (Rankine), for brittle material: substitute in σ<sub>1</sub>.
answer.pre:
σ<sub>1</sub> = 16M/πd³ + (16/πd³)√(M² + T²) = (32/πd³) × ½[M + √(M² + T²)]
so M<sub>e</sub> = ½[M + √(M² + T²)] and σ<sub>allow</sub> = 32M<sub>e</sub>/(πd³)

answer: M<sub>e</sub> is the bending moment that, acting alone, would cause the same maximum normal stress.
Take the larger, 43.4 mm, and adopt the standard 45 mm. For steel shafts the maximum shear stress theory governs and is the basis of the ASME code; the normal stress theory suits cast iron.

Why two theories: ductile steel yields by shear on 45° planes, so its failure is predicted by the largest shear stress; brittle cast iron breaks by tension, so its failure is predicted by the largest normal stress. For the same M and T, M<sub>e</sub> is always at least half of T<sub>e</sub> plus half of M, so the two theories give similar diameters when M dominates and different ones when T dominates.

Use in design: find the critical section from the bending moment diagram (the section with the largest combination of M and T), multiply by K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> if the ASME code is asked, then use T<sub>e</sub> (and M<sub>e</sub> if asked) at that section.

bank.q: Why must a shaft that is strong enough also be checked for rigidity? Explain torsional and lateral rigidity, the limits used, and show with the line-shaft and rotor examples of this unit how each can govern.
outline: Torsional rigidity θ = TL/(GJ), 584TL/(Gd⁴), 0.25° per metre
Lateral rigidity: deflection and slope at gears and bearings
Critical speed as the dynamic stiffness check
answer: Data from this unit: line shaft 20 kW at 300 rpm, τ<sub>allow</sub> = 40 MPa, G = 79.3 GPa, twist limit 0.25° per metre; rotor shaft 60 mm diameter, 1.2 m span, 25 kg rotor at mid-span, E = 200 GPa.

Strength checks keep stress below an allowable value. Stiffness is a separate property: deflection and twist depend on E, G and the fourth power of d, not on the allowable stress, so a shaft can be safe in stress yet twist or bend too much for the parts it carries.

Torsional rigidity: a torque T twists a length L by θ = TL/(GJ) radians, with J = πd⁴/32. In degrees for a solid shaft, θ = 584TL/(Gd⁴). Too much twist puts gears, cams and timing out of step and lets a long shaft wind up and spring back. A common limit for machine-tool and precision drives is 0.25° per metre; line shafts are allowed more.

Lateral rigidity: bending deflects the shaft by y and tilts it by a slope. Slope at a rolling bearing (guide about 0.001 rad) loads the rollers on one edge; deflection at a gear (a few hundredths of a millimetre) moves the tooth contact and changes backlash. Deflection is found by beam theory: δ = WL³/(48EI) for a central load, Macaulay’s method for stepped shafts.

answer.text: Torsional rigidity governing (20 kW at 300 rpm, τ = 40 MPa, G = 79.3 GPa, 0.25°/m):

answer: The rigidity diameter is half as large again as the strength one, and at 70 mm the stress is less than a quarter of the allowable: twist decided the shaft.

Lateral rigidity and critical speed: the 60 mm shaft on a 1.2 m span with a 25 kg central rotor deflects 0.069 mm (within a 0.08 mm limit), but including the shaft’s own mass its critical speed is only 2908 rpm by Dunkerley’s method. A shaft of the same stress level run at 2900 rpm would whirl.
Remedies: a larger diameter (stiffness rises as d⁴), a shorter span or an extra bearing, or a hollow section, which keeps most of the stiffness for less mass.

Critical speed as the dynamic form of lateral rigidity: N<sub>c</sub> = (60/2π)√(g/δ), so any increase in deflection δ lowers the speed at which the shaft whirls. A shaft can therefore be rejected even when its static deflection is inside the limit.

Check: since θ varies as 1/d⁴, the 70 mm shaft twists 0.25 × (65.8/70)⁴ = 0.195° per metre, matching the direct calculation. A stronger steel would not help, because all steels have nearly the same G and E; only a larger diameter or a shorter span adds stiffness.

bank.q: With neat sketches, describe the common types of keys and explain the two ways a sunk key fails. Find the length of the 14 × 9 key for a 50 mm shaft carrying 20 kW at 600 rpm (τ = 40 MPa, σ<sub>c</sub> = 80 MPa).
outline: Sunk keys: rectangular, square, taper, gib-head, feather
Woodruff, saddle, tangent, round and Kennedy keys
answer: Data for the calculation: 50 mm shaft, 20 kW at 600 rpm, standard rectangular key 14 mm wide and 9 mm high, allowable shear 40 MPa and crushing 80 MPa in the key steel.
A key locks a hub to a shaft. Sketch a shaft end in section with each key (one sketch per type, as in the key figure of this unit).

Sunk keys sit half in the shaft and half in the hub. Rectangular: w = d/4, h = 2w/3, the common case. Square: h = w. Parallel keys have no taper; taper keys (1 in 100 on top) are driven in and held by friction and wedging, often with a gib head for removal. A feather key is fixed to one part and slides in the other, so a gear can move along the shaft.

Woodruff key: a half disc in a curved seat; it self-aligns on tapered shafts but its deep seat weakens the shaft. Saddle keys (flat or hollow) need no shaft keyway and drive by friction only: light duty. Tangent keys: a pair of taper keys at 90° for heavy reversing torque. Round key: a pin in a drilled hole. Kennedy key: two square keys set diagonally.
Shear: the torque gives a force F = 2T/d at the shaft surface. The key can shear along the plane where shaft and hub meet: τ = F/(wl).
Crushing: the side face bearing on the hub is h/2 high, so σ<sub>c</sub> = F/((h/2)l). The design length is the larger of the two lengths.

answer.text: Numbers for the 50 mm shaft, 20 kW at 600 rpm, key 14 × 9:

answer: Moore’s factor for the keyway (depth h/2 = 4.5 mm): e = 1 − 0.2 × 14/50 − 1.1 × 4.5/50 = 0.845, so the keyed shaft has about 84.5 % of the plain shaft’s strength.
Splines for comparison: where torque is high or the hub must slide under load, a splined shaft replaces the key; its torque capacity is T = p n h l R<sub>m</sub>, and it avoids a single deep keyway.
Check: the hub must be at least 40 mm long; a hub of 1.5d = 75 mm is common, which also allows a longer key if a stronger margin is wanted.

bank.q: Compare rigid and flexible couplings. Sketch a protected flange coupling and a bushed-pin flexible coupling, list the checks for each, and say where each is chosen.
outline: Rigid types and when they suit
Protected flange coupling proportions and checks
answer: A coupling joins two shaft ends so torque passes between them, and lets the machines be separated for service.

head: Feature
Rigid
Flexible
rows: allows small parallel, angular, axial error
rubber or spring elements damp it
bushed-pin, Oldham, universal joint, gear, disc

answer: Protected flange coupling (sketch: two keyed cast-iron flanges bolted face to face, rims covering the bolt heads, as in the coupling figure). Proportions for shaft d: hub 2d × 1.5d, bolt circle 3d, outside diameter 4d, flange 0.5d, rim 0.25d.
Its checks follow the torque: shaft τ = 16T/(πd³); key in shear and crushing; hub as a hollow shaft; flange in shear at the hub, τ = 2T/(πD²t); bolts in shear and crushing, F = 2T/(nD<sub>1</sub>).

Bushed-pin coupling (sketch: like a flange coupling, but pins fixed in one flange carry rubber bushes that sit in larger holes of the other flange). The bushes deflect, so they take small misalignment and soften shock.

Its checks: pin force F = 2T/(nD<sub>1</sub>); bush bearing pressure F/(D<sub>b</sub> l<sub>b</sub>) ≤ about 1 N/mm²; pin shear F/(πd²/4); pin bending, M = F × (distance from flange face to bush centre).

answer.pre:
flange coupling, 15 kW at 200 rpm, d = 50 mm: four M10 bolts carry 2387 N each, τ = 30.4 MPa
bushed-pin, 30 kW at 720 rpm: six pins carry 829 N each; pin τ = 5.4 MPa but σ<sub>b</sub> = 61.5 MPa

answer: Choice: a rigid flange coupling where the shafts share one accurately machined bed and alignment holds; a flexible coupling where two separate machines are joined, where foundations settle or heat moves the shafts, or where shock must be softened.

Muff and clamp couplings complete the rigid family: a muff (sleeve) coupling has D = 2d + 13 mm and L = 3.5d and is checked as a hollow shaft; a clamp coupling is split so it can be fitted without moving the shafts. The Oldham coupling takes parallel offset and the universal joint takes large angles; two universal joints at equal angles, in phase, give constant output speed.

Installation: whichever is chosen, the shafts are aligned first with a dial gauge or laser, allowing for the hot growth of the machine, because even a flexible coupling has a rated limit beyond which bearing loads climb.
Check: the bushed pin’s bending stress is more than ten times its shear stress, so an answer that checks only shear passes an unsafe pin.

bank.q: Explain the uniform pressure and uniform wear theories for a friction clutch, derive the torque for each, and compare them for r<sub>o</sub> = 150 mm, r<sub>i</sub> = 100 mm, μ = 0.3, W = 5 kN, two pairs.
answer: Symbols: W axial spring force (N), μ coefficient of friction, r<sub>o</sub> and r<sub>i</sub> outer and inner radii of the friction ring (m), p pressure (N/m²), n number of rubbing pairs (2 for a single plate lined on both faces).

Take a thin ring of radius r and width dr on one friction face. Its area is 2πr dr, the normal force on it p × 2πr dr, the friction force μp2πr dr and its torque μp2πr² dr. Integrate from r<sub>i</sub> to r<sub>o</sub> and multiply by n pairs.

answer.text: Uniform pressure (new, accurately flat lining): p is constant.
answer.pre:
W = p π(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)
T = n ∫ μ p 2π r² dr = n μ p (2π/3)(r<sub>o</sub>³ − r<sub>i</sub>³)
T = (2/3) μ W n (r<sub>o</sub>³ − r<sub>i</sub>³)/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)

answer: Uniform wear: wear depth is proportional to pressure × rubbing speed, and rubbing speed is ωr. After running in, the wear is the same everywhere, so p r = C, a constant, and the largest pressure is at r<sub>i</sub>.

answer.pre:
W = ∫ (C/r) 2π r dr = 2πC(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>), so C = W/(2π(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>))
T = n ∫ μ (C/r) 2π r² dr = n μ π C (r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²)
T = μ W n (r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2

answer: The friction radius is (2/3)(r<sub>o</sub>³ − r<sub>i</sub>³)/(r<sub>o</sub>² − r<sub>i</sub>²) for uniform pressure and (r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2 for uniform wear.

answer.text: Numbers (r<sub>o</sub> = 0.15 m, r<sub>i</sub> = 0.10 m, μ = 0.3, W = 5000 N, n = 2):
answer.pre:
uniform wear: T = 0.3 × 5000 × 2 × 0.125 = 375 N·m
uniform pressure: T = 2000 × 0.002375/0.0125 = 380 N·m
p<sub>max</sub> (wear) = 5000/(2π × 0.10 × 0.05) = 0.159 MPa at r<sub>i</sub>

answer: Uniform pressure puts more force at large radius, so it predicts the larger torque. A clutch spends nearly all its life worn in, so the designer uses uniform wear, the lower and safer figure; uniform pressure fits only a brand-new lining.

Effect on design: because uniform wear gives a smaller torque for the same W, a clutch designed by it will still carry the rated torque after its lining has worn in; designing by uniform pressure would overrate it by a few per cent.
Check: the two differ by only 1.3 % here because r<sub>o</sub>/r<sub>i</sub> = 1.5 is close to 1; the closer the radii, the smaller the gap.

bank.q: A solid shaft of 60 mm diameter transmits 25 kW at 400 rpm and carries a bending moment of 900 N·m at its critical section. By the ASME code with S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa and S<sub>ut</sub> = 450 MPa and steady load (K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> = 1), find the factor of safety, with and without a keyway.
outline: Allowable shear stress by the code
answer: Data: d = 60 mm, P = 25 kW, N = 400 rpm, M = 900 N·m, S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa, S<sub>ut</sub> = 450 MPa, K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> = 1 (steady load). The factor of safety is taken as the code allowable shear stress divided by the working maximum shear stress.

Method: the ASME code uses the maximum shear stress theory with τ = 16√((K<sub>b</sub> M)² + (K<sub>t</sub> T)²)/(πd³) and an allowable shear stress equal to the smaller of 0.30S<sub>yt</sub> and 0.18S<sub>ut</sub>, reduced by 25 % for a keyway.

answer.text: Allowable shear stress by the code:
Equivalent torque and shear stress (K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> = 1):

answer: Factor of safety on the code allowable: n = 75/25.5 = 2.95.
With a keyway the code allowable falls by a quarter, to 0.75 × 75 = 56.25 MPa, so n = 56.25/25.5 = 2.21.

Note on the meaning: the code values 0.30S<sub>yt</sub> and 0.18S<sub>ut</sub> already contain a margin against yield and fatigue, so a factor of 2.95 on them is a large reserve; the shaft could carry about three times the load before reaching the code limit.

If the duty had shock, the factors K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> would raise T<sub>e</sub>: with K<sub>b</sub> = 1.5 and K<sub>t</sub> = 1.0, T<sub>e</sub> = √(1350² + 596.8²) = 1476 N·m, τ = 34.8 MPa, and n with a keyway would be 56.25/34.8 = 1.62.

Diameter needed at the code limit (for comparison): with a keyway, d³ = 16 × 1 079 900/(π × 56.25) = 97 780 mm³, d = 46.1 mm. The 60 mm shaft is about 30 % larger in diameter than the code needs for steady load.
Check: τ = 25.5 MPa and the code limit 75 MPa give 75/25.5 = 2.94 to 2.95; the answer is consistent with the rounded stress.

bank.q: A solid shaft and a hollow shaft with d<sub>i</sub>/d<sub>o</sub> = 0.6 must each transmit 1 kN·m at an allowable shear stress of 60 MPa. Find both sizes and the ratio of their masses, and comment.
answer: Data: T = 1 kN·m = 10⁶ N·mm, τ<sub>allow</sub> = 60 MPa, k = d<sub>i</sub>/d<sub>o</sub> = 0.6, same material and length. Torsion alone, so τ = 16T/(πd³) for the solid shaft and τ = 16T/(πd<sub>o</sub>³(1 − k⁴)) for the hollow one, since Z<sub>p</sub> = πd<sub>o</sub>³(1 − k⁴)/16.
The ratio of diameters is d<sub>o</sub>/d = ∛(1/(1 − k⁴)) = 1.047: removing the core costs only 13 % of the strength, so the outside grows by under 5 %.

answer.text: Mass ratio for the same length and material = ratio of areas:

answer: The hollow shaft is about 30 % lighter for the same torque and stress. The core near the axis carries little shear (stress grows with radius), so removing it costs little strength but saves much mass.

The hollow shaft is also stiffer per kilogram, so its critical speed is higher; this is why propeller shafts of ships and vehicles and large turbine shafts are hollow. Against it: boring costs money, and a hollow shaft needs a slightly larger outside diameter and larger bearings.
In practice adopt standard sizes: solid 45 mm; hollow 48 mm outside with a 28 mm bore (k = 0.58) or the nearest tube size, then recheck τ.

Stiffness comparison: the polar second moment J is proportional to d⁴ for the solid shaft and d<sub>o</sub>⁴(1 − k⁴) for the hollow one: 43.95⁴ = 3.731 × 10⁶ mm⁴ against 46.03⁴ × 0.8704 = 3.908 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The hollow shaft is about 5 % stiffer in torsion while 30 % lighter.
Strength-to-weight: torque per unit area is 10⁶/1517 = 659 N·mm per mm² for the solid shaft (area 1517 mm²) and 10⁶/1065 = 939 N·mm per mm² for the hollow one (area 1065 mm²), 42 % more.
Check: hollow τ at d<sub>o</sub> = 46.03 mm: 16 × 10⁶/(π × 46.03³ × 0.8704) = 60.0 MPa.

bank.q: A 50 mm steel shaft (E = 200 GPa) on bearings 1 m apart carries 400 N at mid-span and 250 N at 0.3 m from the left bearing. Find the deflections under the loads and estimate the first critical speed by Rayleigh’s method; check it by Dunkerley’s method, neglecting the shaft’s mass.
outline: I and the point-load deflection formula
answer: Data: d = 50 mm, L = 1.0 m, E = 200 GPa, W<sub>1</sub> = 400 N at x = 0.5 m, W<sub>2</sub> = 250 N at x = 0.3 m, g = 9.81 m/s². The shaft is treated as simply supported and massless.
For a load W at distance a from the left bearing (b = L − a), the deflection at x ≤ a is y = Wbx(L² − b² − x²)/(6EIL), and by symmetry the same form from the right for x ≥ a.

answer.text: Dunkerley (each load alone, its own deflection):

answer: Rayleigh gives 2165 rpm, slightly above the true value; Dunkerley gives 2138 rpm, slightly below. The true first critical speed lies between, and the two agree within 1.3 %.

Design rule: keep the running speed at least 20 to 25 % away, below about 1600 to 1700 rpm here, or above about 2700 rpm with a quick run-through. Bearing flexibility and the shaft’s own mass would lower N<sub>c</sub> a little further; gyroscopic effects of discs are ignored.

Why the two differ: Rayleigh’s method assumes the static deflection curve as the mode shape, which is slightly stiffer than the true mode, so it overestimates; Dunkerley’s method ignores the coupling between the loads’ deflections, which underestimates.
Check: Dunkerley ≤ Rayleigh, as it must be (2138 < 2165).

bank.q: A 50 mm shaft transmits 40 kW at 500 rpm to a hub through a square key of side d/4. The key steel has τ = 40 MPa and σ<sub>c</sub> = 80 MPa. Find the key length, the hub length, and compare with a key as strong as the shaft.
outline: Key as strong as the shaft
answer: Data: d = 50 mm, P = 40 kW, N = 500 rpm, square key w = h = d/4, τ = 40 MPa, σ<sub>c</sub> = 80 MPa. The key force acts at the shaft surface, radius d/2; shear acts on the area w × l and crushing on the half height in the hub, (h/2) × l.
Square key: w = h = d/4 = 12.5 mm (a standard table would give 14 × 9 for this shaft; the question fixes a square key).
The two lengths are equal because the key is square and σ<sub>c</sub> = 2τ: the crushing area (h/2)l is half the shear area wl, and the allowable crushing stress is twice the shear stress.

Adopt l = 65 mm: τ = 30 558/(12.5 × 65) = 37.6 MPa and σ<sub>c</sub> = 30 558/(6.25 × 65) = 75.2 MPa, both within limits. The hub must be at least 65 mm; with the common 1.5d it is 75 mm, and the key can run its full length.
Key as strong as the shaft (same τ): equate key shear capacity wlτd/2 to shaft capacity πd³τ/16, which gives l = πd²/(8w) = π × 50²/(8 × 12.5) = 78.5 mm, that is 1.571d.

So a 78.5 mm key would match the shaft’s own torsional strength. The 65 mm key is enough for the 40 kW load, but would fail first in an overload; this is often wanted, as a cheap key is easier to replace than a shaft.

Keyway effect on the shaft: with a keyway depth h/2 = 6.25 mm, Moore’s factor is e = 1 − 0.2 × 12.5/50 − 1.1 × 6.25/50 = 0.8125, so the keyed shaft has about 81 % of the plain shaft’s strength, and the shaft stress should be compared with 0.81 × 40 = 32.5 MPa: 31.1 MPa just passes.
Check: shaft stress at this load is 16 × 763 944/(π × 50³) = 31.1 MPa ≤ 40 MPa, so the 50 mm shaft itself is adequate.

bank.q: Design a cast-iron protected flange coupling for a 45 mm steel shaft driven by a 30 kW, 720 rpm motor. Take a service factor of 1.25; shaft, key and bolts 40 MPa in shear and 80 MPa in crushing; cast iron 15 MPa in shear; four bolts. State every dimension.
answer: Data and assumptions: P = 30 kW, N = 720 rpm, d = 45 mm, service factor 1.25 for a motor-driven machine with moderate shock; steel shaft, key and bolts with τ = 40 MPa, σ<sub>c</sub> = 80 MPa; cast-iron flanges with τ = 15 MPa; four bolts fitted in reamed holes so they act in shear; usual proportions for the hub, flange and rim.
Shaft: τ = 16T<sub>d</sub>/(πd³) = 16 × 497 360/(π × 45³) = 27.8 MPa ≤ 40 MPa, so the 45 mm shaft is safe.

Proportions for d = 45 mm: hub diameter D = 2d = 90 mm, hub length 1.5d = 67.5 mm (take 70 mm), bolt circle D<sub>1</sub> = 3d = 135 mm, outside diameter 4d = 180 mm, flange t = 0.5d = 22.5 mm, protecting rim 0.25d ≈ 11.5 mm.
Hub as a hollow shaft: τ = 16T<sub>d</sub> D/(π(D⁴ − d⁴)) = 16 × 497 360 × 90/(π(90⁴ − 45⁴)) = 3.71 MPa ≤ 15 MPa.

answer.text: Key: standard 14 × 9 for a 45 mm shaft, length = hub length 70 mm.

answer: Flange shear at the hub: τ = 2T<sub>d</sub>/(πD²t) = 2 × 497 360/(π × 90² × 22.5) = 1.74 MPa ≤ 15 MPa.

Sketch to draw in the answer: a half-section through both flanges showing the shafts, keys, hubs, flanges with the spigot and recess for alignment, the bolts on the pitch circle, and the protecting rims covering the bolt heads and nuts, as in the coupling figure of this unit.
Check: every stress is within its limit; the key in crushing (70.2 of 80 MPa) is the most highly used part, so it is the first to watch if the duty rises.

bank.q: A single-plate clutch, both sides effective, must transmit 15 kW at 1000 rpm. μ = 0.3, the largest lining pressure is 0.1 MPa and r<sub>o</sub>/r<sub>i</sub> = 1.4. Find r<sub>i</sub>, r<sub>o</sub> and the spring force by uniform wear theory.
outline: Uniform wear: p<sub>max</sub> at r<sub>i</sub>, W = 2πp<sub>max</sub> r<sub>i</sub>(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>)
answer: Data: P = 15 kW, N = 1000 rpm, μ = 0.3, p<sub>max</sub> = 0.1 MPa (N/mm²), r<sub>o</sub> = 1.4r<sub>i</sub>, n = 2. Uniform wear theory is used because it is the run-in condition and gives the lower torque.

Uniform wear: p r = C, with the largest pressure at r<sub>i</sub>, so C = p<sub>max</sub> r<sub>i</sub> and W = 2πC(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>) = 2πp<sub>max</sub> r<sub>i</sub>(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>).

answer.pre:
T = μWn(r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)/2 = μ n π p<sub>max</sub> r<sub>i</sub>(r<sub>o</sub> − r<sub>i</sub>)(r<sub>o</sub> + r<sub>i</sub>)
  = 0.3 × 2 × π × 0.1 × r<sub>i</sub> × 0.4r<sub>i</sub> × 2.4r<sub>i</sub> = 0.18096 r<sub>i</sub>³ (N·mm, r<sub>i</sub> in mm)
r<sub>i</sub>³ = 143 240/0.18096 = 791 550 mm³, r<sub>i</sub> = 92.5 mm, r<sub>o</sub> = 129.5 mm

answer: Round up: r<sub>i</sub> = 95 mm and r<sub>o</sub> = 133 mm (ratio 1.4).

answer.text: Spring force and torque with the rounded radii:

answer: The largest pressure stays at 0.1 MPa at r<sub>i</sub> (it is set by W), and the pressure at r<sub>o</sub> is 0.1 × 95/133 = 0.071 MPa.

Both faces count: with one side only the radii would have to grow by ∛2 = 1.26 times. The heat from slipping must also be checked: at a 0.5 s engagement from 1000 rpm relative speed, E ≈ 155 × (104.7/2) × 0.5 = 4060 J per start.
Pressure check: the spring force 2268 N spread over the ring area π(133² − 95²) = 27 220 mm² gives a mean pressure of 0.083 MPa, below the 0.1 MPa peak at r<sub>i</sub>, as uniform wear requires.

Comparison with uniform pressure for the same radii and W: T = (2/3) × 0.3 × 2268 × 2 × (133³ − 95³)/(133² − 95²) = 156.6 N·m, about 1 % higher, so the choice of theory changes the size only slightly when r<sub>o</sub>/r<sub>i</sub> is 1.4.
Check: the unrounded r<sub>i</sub> = 92.5 mm gives W = 2150 N and T = 143.2 N·m exactly, confirming the algebra.

bank.q: Design the I-section connecting rod for a petrol engine: bore 90 mm, peak gas pressure 5 MPa, length 300 mm between centres, factor of safety 6, σ<sub>c</sub> = 330 MPa, a = 1/7500. Find also the piston pin (p<sub>b</sub> = 12.5 MPa, l/d = 2) and the crankpin (p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa, l/d = 1.25).
outline: Rankine’s formula and the quadratic in t²
answer: Data: bore D = 90 mm, p<sub>max</sub> = 5 MPa, L = 300 mm, factor of safety 6 on the buckling load, σ<sub>c</sub> = 330 MPa, Rankine constant a = 1/7500, piston pin p<sub>b</sub> = 12.5 MPa with l/d = 2, crankpin p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa with l/d = 1.25. Near top dead centre the rod is almost in line with the cylinder, so the rod force is taken equal to the gas force.

I-section with flange and web t, B = 4t, H = 5t: A = 11t², I<sub>xx</sub> = 419t⁴/12, k<sub>xx</sub>² = I<sub>xx</sub>/A = 3.17t². The rod is pinned in the plane of motion (length L about xx) and nearly fixed out of it (L/2 about yy); since I<sub>xx</sub> = 3.2I<sub>yy</sub>, design about xx.
Taper: H = 40 mm at the centre; about 1.1H to 1.25H = 44 to 50 mm at the big end and 0.75H to 0.9H = 30 to 36 mm at the small end, keeping B = 32 mm.
Other checks a full answer names: inertia (whipping) bending M = m ω²rL²/(9√3) at the top speed, and the big-end cap bolts for the inertia force at top dead centre of the exhaust stroke.

Sketch to draw: the I-section with t, 4t and 5t marked, and the rod elevation with the small end, the tapering shank and the big end with its cap and two bolts, as in the connecting-rod figure of this unit.
Check: the 8 mm section gives 219 kN against 191 kN required, so the factor of safety 6.9 is above the 6 asked.

bank.q: A single-cylinder engine (bore 90 mm, peak pressure 5 MPa) has a centre crankshaft. The crankpin centre is 90 mm from the left main bearing and 110 mm from the right one. Design the crankpin for the crank at top dead centre (p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa, l/d = 1, σ<sub>b</sub> = 70 MPa) and check a web 100 mm wide and 35 mm thick. Ignore the flywheel.
outline: Gas force at top dead centre
Crankpin by bearing pressure, then bending
answer: Data: F<sub>p</sub> from D = 90 mm and p<sub>max</sub> = 5 MPa; crankpin centre 90 mm from the left bearing (b<sub>1</sub>) and 110 mm from the right (b<sub>2</sub>); crankpin p<sub>b</sub> = 10 MPa with l<sub>c</sub> = d<sub>c</sub>; allowable bending stress 70 MPa; web 100 mm wide and 35 mm thick. At top dead centre the crank, rod and cylinder are in line, so the full gas force acts radially on the crankpin.

answer.pre: F<sub>p</sub> = (π/4) × 90² × 5 = 31 809 N (along the crank, no torque at top dead centre)

answer.text: Reactions (moments about each bearing, b = 200 mm):
answer.pre: R<sub>1</sub> = F<sub>p</sub> × 110/200 = 17 495 N (left);  R<sub>2</sub> = F<sub>p</sub> × 90/200 = 14 314 N (right)
d<sub>c</sub> × l<sub>c</sub> × 10 = 31 809 with l<sub>c</sub> = d<sub>c</sub> → d<sub>c</sub> = 56.4 mm

M = R<sub>1</sub> × 90 = 1 574 530 N·mm
at 56.4 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd<sub>c</sub>³) = 89.4 MPa > 70 MPa
d<sub>c</sub>³ = 32 × 1 574 530/(π × 70) = 229 120 mm³ → d<sub>c</sub> = 61.2 mm, adopt 62 mm

answer: Check at 62 mm × 62 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 32 × 1 574 530/(π × 62³) = 67.3 MPa ≤ 70 and p<sub>b</sub> = 31 809/(62 × 62) = 8.3 MPa ≤ 10. Bending governed, not bearing pressure.

answer.text: Left web (w = 100 mm, t = 35 mm): it carries R<sub>1</sub> in compression and in bending about its thickness, with the arm from the bearing centre to the web centre, 90 − 62/2 − 35/2 = 41.5 mm.

answer: The second position, at the crank angle of maximum torque (about 25° to 35° after top dead centre), must also be checked: the rod force splits into tangential and radial parts, the crankpin and the shaft beside the web carry bending and torsion together, and the shaft diameter there comes from √(M² + T²).

Sketch to draw: the crankshaft as a beam on two main bearings with the crankpin load F<sub>p</sub> between them at 90 mm and 110 mm, the reactions R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>, and the triangular bending moment diagram peaking at 1 574 530 N·mm under the crankpin.
Check: the left reaction is the larger because the crankpin is nearer the left bearing, and R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> = 31 809 N.

bank.q: A shaft that is strong enough on paper keeps cracking at its keyway within weeks. Analyse the likely causes, using the stress and rigidity ideas of this unit, and recommend design changes.
outline: Keyway stress concentration and Moore’s factor
Vibration from rigidity and critical speed
answer: What is known: the shaft passed the static check by the equivalent torque, yet cracks start at the keyway within weeks. The analysis asks why a static pass did not prevent the failure and what the design missed.

A crack in weeks is fatigue, not static overload: the shaft passed a static check with T<sub>e</sub> but failed under millions of stress reversals. Rotating bending reverses fully every turn, and torque often fluctuates.

The keyway is the weak spot. Its sharp root corners raise the local stress two to three times above nominal; Moore’s factor for the 14 × 9 keyway in a 50 mm shaft is 0.845 even before fatigue is considered. A profile keyway cut by an end mill has a sharper end than a sled-runner keyway.

Code allowances may have been skipped: the ASME code cuts the allowable shear stress by 25 % for a keyway and raises M and T by K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> for shock. A design with K<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>t</sub> = 1 for a shock-loaded drive, or with no keyway reduction, is undersized by 25 to 50 %.
Shock or misalignment adds load: a rigid coupling to a misaligned machine, or a hub loose on its key, turns every revolution into a hammer blow on the keyway side.

Rigidity and critical speed: a slender shaft that deflects at a gear, or runs near N<sub>c</sub>, vibrates, and the vibration adds bending stress cycles. The shaft of the critical-speed example runs safely below 2180 rpm but would whirl near 2900 rpm.

answer.text: Recommended changes, in order of effect:

head: Change
Why
rows: stress falls as 1/d³; stiffness rises as d⁴
Splines or a keyless locking device
Correct K<sub>b</sub>, K<sub>t</sub> and the keyway factor
Flexible coupling, alignment, tight key fit
Fatigue check with Goodman or Soderberg
uses the endurance limit, not yield

answer: How to confirm: inspect the fracture face for beach marks (fatigue) starting at a keyway corner, measure the actual torque and vibration in service, and check the key fit and coupling alignment before redesigning.
Check: raising the shaft from 50 to 55 mm cuts the nominal stress by (50/55)³ = 0.75, a 25 % reduction, which alone restores the margin the code’s keyway allowance asks for.

bank.q: A motor drives a gearbox whose shaft centre is 0.3 mm off line and 0.2° skewed. Evaluate a rigid flange coupling against a bushed-pin coupling for a 30 kW, 720 rpm drive, using this unit’s numbers.
outline: What misalignment does to a rigid coupling
How the bushed pin absorbs it
Bushed-pin numbers: pin force, bush length, pin stresses
answer: Data: misalignment 0.3 mm parallel and 0.2° angular; drive 30 kW at 720 rpm, torque 397.9 N·m; candidate couplings: a rigid flange coupling and a bushed-pin coupling with six 14 mm pins on a 160 mm circle and 30 mm bushes.

With a rigid coupling the two shafts are forced into line. The 0.3 mm offset and 0.2° angle are taken up by bending the shafts and loading the bearings, and the bending reverses every revolution, so the bearings see an extra cyclic radial load and the shafts an extra bending stress cycle at 12 Hz (720 rpm).

Rolling bearing life falls roughly as the cube of the load (for ball bearings), so even a modest extra radial load shortens life sharply; misalignment also shows as vibration at once and twice the shaft speed, and as coupling bolt fretting.

A bushed-pin coupling lets the rubber bushes deflect: offset and angle become small rubber strains, and only a small restoring force reaches the bearings. The rubber also damps torque shock at start-up.

answer.text: Sizing the bushed pin (six pins on a 160 mm circle, 14 mm pins, 30 mm bushes, load 20 mm from the flange):
answer.pre:
T = 397.9 N·m;  F = 2T/(nD<sub>1</sub>) = 829 N per pin
bush: l<sub>b</sub> = 829/(1 × 30) = 27.6 → 30 mm
pin: τ = 5.4 MPa, σ<sub>b</sub> = 32 × 16 580/(π × 14³) = 61.5 MPa, τ<sub>max</sub> = 31.2 MPa

answer: These are modest stresses for a steel pin, and the rubber rated for 1 N/mm² is the limiting element; maker tables give the allowable offset and angle for each size, typically a few tenths of a millimetre and under a degree, which covers this case.

Cost and upkeep: the rigid coupling is cheaper and needs no spares; the bushed pin needs bush replacement every few years. Neither replaces alignment: correct the error first, then choose the coupling for what remains after thermal growth.

Effect on critical speed: a rigid coupling makes the two shafts act as one stiffer, longer beam, while a flexible coupling separates them dynamically; either way, the shaft critical speeds should be checked against 720 rpm with the coupling mass included.

Recommendation: the bushed-pin coupling, after aligning the machines as closely as practicable. Check: its pins run at 31.2 MPa maximum shear and its bushes at 0.92 N/mm² with 30 mm length (829/(30 × 30)), both within limits.

glossary.def: A rotating member that transmits torque and carries gears, pulleys or rotors.
A member that supports rotating parts but transmits no torque; designed for bending only.
A short shaft, such as the main shaft of a machine tool.
T<sub>e</sub> = √(M² + T²): the torque that alone gives the same maximum shear stress as M and T together.
M<sub>e</sub> = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]: the moment that alone gives the same maximum normal stress.
K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>t</sub> in the ASME code, multiplying the bending moment and torque for the type of loading.
GJ; the resistance of a shaft to twist, which sets the angle θ = TL/(GJ).
The speed at which a shaft’s rotation matches its lateral natural frequency and whirl peaks.
Large lateral bending of a rotating shaft near its critical speed.
An estimate of the critical speed from the separate critical speeds of each load and the shaft; slightly low.
An estimate of the critical speed from the static deflection curve under all loads; slightly high.
A key fitted half in the shaft and half in the hub keyway.
A parallel key that lets the hub slide along the shaft while turning with it.
A half-disc key in a curved seat, used on tapered shaft ends.
A key with no shaft keyway that drives by friction alone.
One of several teeth cut on a shaft that mesh with grooves in a hub.
A rigid coupling: a sleeve keyed over both shaft ends.
A rigid flange coupling whose rims cover the bolt heads and nuts.
A flexible coupling with rubber-bushed pins that absorb small misalignment and shock.
A coupling with a tongued centre disc that allows a parallel offset of the shafts.
A cross-and-yoke joint that transmits torque between shafts at an angle.
A multiplier on the rated torque for shock and the duty of the driven machine.
The run-in state of a friction face in which pressure × radius is constant.
Loss of braking torque as hot lining loses friction.
A brake in which friction alone holds the block on, so it will not release.
A column formula combining crushing and buckling: P = σ<sub>c</sub> A/(1 + a(L/k)²).
Bending of a connecting rod by the inertia of its own mass at high speed.
A crankshaft with the crankpin between two main bearings.
